summary.oneLiner: Karma Energy Limited is a small Indian renewable-power generator operating about 30.50 MW of wind farms and selling wind power to state utilities and third parties.
summary.business: Karma Energy is engaged in renewable power generation through wind farm development and operation; the Board's report notes the Company is in the field of wind farm development and not manufacturing. It operates wind farms in Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra and sells generation to State Electricity Boards / utilities and, where open access permits, to third parties. The Company has no subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures, and there was no change in the business of the company during the year as compared to the previous year.

endMarkets: State electricity utilities / State Electricity Boards (India)|Third-party open-access power buyers|Tamil Nadu|Maharashtra

currentContext.strengths: Debt free: the Company prepaid in December 2022 the financial assistance obtained in earlier years and, as at the Balance Sheet date, does not have any Secured Borrowing; MD&A states it 'is now debt free for past 2-3 years'.|Improved cash collection discipline from state utilities via the Ministry of Power's 'Prapti' online portal, which the Company says forces State Electricity Companies to settle dues on due date and has facilitated regular cash flow.|Active portfolio pruning: the Company closed down loss-making and low-tariff wind farms in Andhra Pradesh and a unit in Tamil Nadu, and retired wind mills that had outlived their technical life.
currentContext.strategies: Cost reduction, tight cash flow management and pursuit of policy changes to mitigate the sector downturn.|Rationalise the fleet: close loss-making and low-tariff wind farms (Andhra Pradesh, one unit in Tamil Nadu) and retire wind mills that have outlived their technical life where continued operation is uneconomical.|Stay debt free by using improved realisation of generation dues from state utilities, having pre-paid the bank term loans.|Use the Ministry of Power's 'Prapti' online portal, registering invoice details so State Electricity Companies settle dues on due date, to keep cash flow regular and tackle liquidity mismatch.
currentContext.expansion: The annual report discloses no expansion or new capex project. The direction is the opposite: the MD&A states the Company now has about 30.50 MW of power generating wind farms and had closed down loss-making and low-tariff wind farms in Andhra Pradesh and a unit in Tamil Nadu, and that wind mills which have outlived their technical life — where continued operation even with good operation and maintenance may prove uneconomical because tariffs remain fixed with no adjustment for inflation or actual repair and establishment costs — have been retired. Management observes that the huge outlay needed to meet Central Government renewable targets means only big business houses with deep pockets are entering the Green Power space, and that delays by state utilities, State Electricity Regulatory Commissions and higher judicial authorities are impeding future projects. Existing wind farms are located at Theni and Tirunelveli in Tamil Nadu and Beed and Satara in Maharashtra. The Board's report confirms there was no change in the business of the company during the year and that no new business was commenced or products introduced in FY 2025-26.

risks.risk: Total dependence on renewable-energy policy of Centre and State Governments and on State Electricity Regulatory Commissions
risks.note: MD&A states 'The performance of the Company is directly linked to the Renewable Energy Policies of both Centre and State Governments, effectiveness of Nodal Agencies and formulation of encouraging policies and implementation thereof by State Electricity Regulatory Commissions.' The Company has no control over the single variable that sets its revenue.

MD&A says in many states tariffs 'have not being encouraging' and that tariff remains fixed for many years with no adjustment to inflation or the factual cost of repairs and establishment costs, so ageing wind mills 'may prove uneconomical' even with good operation and maintenance.

MD&A: 'sale to third parties are being discouraged by imposing high open access charges under one pretext or other', which the Company reads as continued regulatory support for conventional energy and which closes off the higher-realisation merchant channel.

risks.risk: Receivable delays from state utilities against a fixed cost base
risks.note: MD&A: 'In the wind power business the expenses are more or less fixed, the delayed receipt of generation proceeds necessitate that company has to resort to temporary borrowings to tide over the mismatch. This is also a concern as it has to bear the brunt of finance cost.' Partially mitigated by the Ministry of Power's 'Prapti' portal, which has helped the Company tackle liquidity issues.

risks.risk: Inordinate delays in adjudication by regulators, APTEL and High Courts
risks.note: MD&A: 'inordinate delays in adjudication of the matters by Electricity Regulatory Commission, Appellate Tribunal for Electricity and even High courts result in acute pressure on the Company due to huge mismatch in inflow and outflow of funds', and the same delays are 'impeding the future projects'.

risks.risk: Sub-scale position in a sector that has consolidated toward large players
risks.note: MD&A repeatedly states that 'present environment in Green Energy is only for Big Players with deep pockets developing in terms of thousands of MW', that such houses can absorb running losses and negotiate better with utilities due to their size, and that many small and medium entities that entered two decades back have closed their units. Karma operates about 30.50 MW.

risks.risk: Ageing asset base driving volatile operation, maintenance and repair costs
risks.note: MD&A's ratio commentary attributes the year's loss and the adverse interest coverage and net profit margin to 'higher Operation and Maintenance Costs, repairs to Wind mills at different sites' despite improved turnover; wind mills that outlived their technical life have had to be retired and units in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu were closed.

The Corporate Governance Report discloses a SEBI adjudication and settlement process over deviations from the Listing Regulations, with an order issued on 10th July 2025 imposing a penalty which the Company remitted, and BSE notices received on 6th April 2026 for non-compliance with Regulation 17(1) of SEBI LODR for the quarters ended 30th September 2024 and 31st December 2024, with penalties since paid.
